props.title: Sexy Beast
props.initialSlug: Ex-gangster's peaceful retirement upended by violent past

sections.content: **Sexy Beast** (2000) revolutionized the British gangster film by subverting every expectation of the genre. Ray Winstone plays Gal Dove, a retired criminal lounging in Spanish paradise until Ben Kingsley's Don Logan erupts into his life like a verbal terrorist. Kingsley's volcanic performance redefined screen menace - no guns needed, just psychological warfare through relentless manipulation. Where films like **Lock, Stock and Two Smoking Barrels** (1998) played London crime for laughs, Sexy Beast brings suffocating dread and existential terror to the Costa del Sol.

sections.content: Director Jonathan Glazer's background in music videos and commercials brings a hypnotic visual style that would later flourish in **Under the Skin** (2013). The surreal opening sequence with the boulder and demonic rabbit sets up the film's exploration of subconscious fears breaking through to paradise. Like **Performance** (1970) before it, Sexy Beast uses criminal elements to explore identity and masculinity in crisis.

Kingsley's Don Logan represents a radical departure from the typical British gangster archetype seen in films like **Get Carter** (1971) or **The Italian Job** (1969). Instead of suave professionalism, he embodies pure psychological terrorism through verbal abuse and manipulation. His performance influenced a generation of screen villains, including Tom Hardy's portrayal in **Bronson** (2008). SUBHEAD: The New Wave of British Crime Films

movies.title: In Bruges
movies.slug: Hitmen hide out in Belgium in this darkly comic crime film that similarly blends violence, humor and existential crisis

sections.content: Sexy Beast arrived amid a renaissance in British crime cinema, following Guy Ritchie's **Snatch** (2000) and preceding **44 Inch Chest** (2009) - another Ray Winstone vehicle exploring masculine crisis through crime genre conventions. The film elevated the genre beyond cockney caricatures and witty violence, diving deep into psychological horror territory while maintaining crime film frameworks.
